title: Marketing Research Digest — Advertising — 2026-11-06

Journal of Empirical Generalisations in Marketing Science
Marketing Science Institute Working Paper Series

studies.title: Go dark for one quarter, lose a tenth of your market share
studies.paper_title: Quarterly advertising pauses and market share
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 7,029 brand-quarter observations covering more than 1,000 brands in 22 product categories, comparing market share for brands that advertised continuously against those that paused. A single quarter with no advertising was associated with an average market share decline of about 10%, and four consecutive quarters off air with a decline of about 14%. The pattern supports continuity and recency planning rather than concentrating media around demand peaks.
studies.why_it_matters: Budget cuts and seasonal flighting are usually framed as efficiency moves, but this gives finance-facing marketers a concrete number for what a dark quarter costs in share.
studies.story_angle_primary: Use the figure as ammunition in budget negotiations: before approving a quarter off air, model the share erosion against the cash saved, and consider whether a reduced-weight continuous schedule beats a full stop. Worth replicating inside your own category data, since averages across 22 categories may not match yours.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Brands you stop hearing about tend to quietly slip down the shopping list — a reminder that advertising works partly by keeping a name mentally available, not just by making a pitch.
studies.caveats: Observational data, so pauses may coincide with other problems (distribution loss, price moves, declining brands cutting spend); the abstract does not specify countries, time period or how confounds were handled.
studies.verdict_notes: Headline numbers (-10%, -14%), sample (7,029 observations, 1,000+ brands, 22 categories) and the continuity/recency framing all match. One design detail is described more specifically than the abstract supports.

studies.title: Clever ads make mass brands look cool — and do nothing for luxury ones
studies.paper_title: Wit-based humor in advertising: brand coolness in luxury and non-luxury brands
studies.the_study: Three experiments tested consumer reactions to ads using wit-based (cognitive) humor versus non-humorous ads across eyewear, automobiles and headphones, with both a fictitious "Brand X" and real brands including Honda and BMW. Witty humor raised perceptions of the brand as "cool," which in turn lifted word-of-mouth intentions and purchase intentions — but only for non-luxury brands. For luxury brands, the coolness route did not pay off.
studies.why_it_matters: Humor is one of the cheapest levers in creative, and this suggests its payoff depends on where a brand sits on the luxury ladder rather than on execution quality alone.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are a challenger or mainstream brand, test wit-driven creative as a coolness play and measure coolness explicitly as a mid-funnel metric; if you are premium or luxury, treat clever humor as a risk to be pretested rather than a default route to relevance.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Why a smart joke from a mass-market car brand lands as charming, while the same joke from a prestige badge can feel off — audiences hold expensive brands to a different tonal standard.
studies.caveats: Lab experiments with stated intentions rather than real purchases; sample sizes and recruitment source not reported in the abstract; three categories only.
studies.verdict_notes: Three experiments, the three categories, Brand X plus Honda/BMW, the coolness mechanism and the non-luxury-only boundary condition are all reported faithfully; intentions-vs-behavior and missing sample sizes are flagged in Caveats.

studies.title: Crowded food ads make the food look more fattening
studies.paper_title: Denser Advertising Design, Higher Food Calories: How Visual Density Affects Consumer Responses to Food Advertising
studies.the_study: Across four experiments plus a secondary data study, researchers manipulated the visual density of food advertising — how much is packed into the frame — and found that denser designs made consumers perceive the food as higher in calories. Dense layouts improved responses when more calories were desirable (indulgence goals, feeling the urge to splurge, indulgence-positioned products) and hurt responses when fewer calories were desirable (health goals, health-positioned products).
studies.why_it_matters: Layout density is a design decision usually made on esthetic grounds, but it appears to function as an implicit calorie claim that either reinforces or contradicts a product's positioning.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit whether your food creative's visual busyness matches its positioning — airy, sparse layouts for better-for-you lines, dense and loaded frames for indulgence — and consider A/B testing density as a variable alongside copy and imagery.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Your sense of how caloric a dish is can be nudged by nothing more than how crowded the picture is, which is worth knowing when you are scrolling a delivery app.
studies.caveats: Mostly experimental with perceptions and intentions rather than observed purchases; sample sizes and recruitment sources not reported in the abstract; secondary data study details unspecified.
studies.verdict_notes: Study count (four experiments + one secondary data study), the density-to-perceived-calories effect and the two-sided moderation are correct; one moderator is mislabeled.

studies.title: When a chatbot says "I," personalized ads start to feel creepy
studies.paper_title: Agency cues in personalized chatbot advertising: the role of grammatical subject framing, privacy concern, and social role
studies.the_study: Two online experiments (N=396 and N=302) varied how personalized a chatbot's ad message was and whether the sentence was framed around the AI ("I") or the consumer ("you"). Under high personalization, AI-subject framing raised privacy concern, which reduced brand attitude and purchase intention; the pattern replicated in a second product category. The damage was worse when the chatbot was positioned as a friend rather than as a servant.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the privacy backlash to conversational AI advertising can be triggered or avoided by grammar at the sentence level — a cheap and testable copy variable.
studies.story_angle_primary: Rewrite highly personalized chatbot and assistant copy to center the customer rather than the AI's agency, and be cautious about buddy-style personas on data-heavy messages; this is a low-cost live test for anyone deploying conversational commerce.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A small clue to why some AI assistants feel helpful and others feel like they are watching you: when the bot foregrounds what it knows and what it is doing, the personalization reads as surveillance.
studies.caveats: Online experiments with hypothetical ads and stated intentions, not real purchases; panel composition and country not specified in the abstract; two product categories.
studies.verdict_notes: Both Ns, the personalization × grammatical-subject manipulation, the moderated mediation via privacy concern, the second-category replication and the friend-vs-servant boundary condition all match the abstract.

studies.title: Rainbow washing worked — even on LGBTQIAPN+ consumers
studies.paper_title: Rainbow Washing Advertising: Experiments with the Reaction of LGBTQIAPN+ Consumers
studies.journal: Journal of Nonprofit & Public Sector Marketing
studies.the_study: Two sequential Brazilian experiments compared a rainbow-washing ad against a neutral ad: an exploratory study (n=20) using eye tracking and implicit attitude measures, and an explanatory study (n=74) using self-reports. The rainbow-washing ad drew more visual attention, produced more positive emotional reactions and better brand evaluations, and participants found it difficult to identify the practice as inauthentic. Exposure to negative media coverage about the brand restored some critical scrutiny and dampened the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the assumption that the targeted community reliably polices performative diversity advertising, and points to media scrutiny rather than consumer vigilance as the real check.
studies.story_angle_primary: Short-term attention metrics on diversity-themed creative can look great while the underlying authenticity gap remains invisible — brands should treat press and watchdog scrutiny, not campaign engagement data, as the signal that matters, and prepare for the effect to reverse once coverage lands.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Even people with the most at stake struggle to tell genuine support from a logo repaint; knowing a brand's record before the campaign is the only reliable defense.
studies.caveats: Very small samples (n=20 and n=74), single country (Brazil), hypothetical ads rather than real purchase behavior, and short exposure horizon.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample sizes, sequential design, measures and the core finding are faithful; the country is not stated in the abstract and one story angle upgrades "mitigating" to "reversing".

studies.title: Your ad platform's own algorithm is corrupting its effectiveness numbers
studies.paper_title: The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
studies.the_study: This Marketing Science paper shows that because ad auctions allocate impressions deterministically, many users have a near-zero or near-one chance of seeing a given ad — violating the overlap condition that observational ad-effect estimates require, and biasing results even when assignment is otherwise unconfounded. The authors reframe the problem as missing data and use matrix completion across multiple campaigns to recover causal effects, validating the approach on simulated and real advertising data and showing improved targeting efficiency.
studies.why_it_matters: Advertisers increasingly accept platform-reported, observational lift numbers as a cheaper substitute for randomized holdouts; this argues those numbers can be systematically wrong precisely because the platform's targeting is good.
studies.story_angle_primary: Ask platforms how their lift estimates handle overlap, and keep randomized holdouts or geo experiments in the measurement mix rather than trusting algorithmically derived attribution — and watch for borrowing-across-campaigns methods entering vendor measurement stacks.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Limited angle for consumers, beyond the irony that the better an ad system gets at showing you only the ads you are likely to respond to, the harder it becomes to prove those ads worked.
studies.caveats: Methodological paper; validation rests on simulations plus one real advertising data set whose source and scope are not described in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: The overlap-violation argument, the missing-data/matrix-completion framing, validation on simulated and real data and the targeting-efficiency claim all match; methodological nature is flagged in Caveats.

studies.title: Bragging vs. earning it: which flavor of pride sells depends on how the ad makes you see yourself
studies.paper_title: The Role of Pride Appeals and Self-Construal in Advertising
studies.journal: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
studies.the_study: Two experiments tested two kinds of pride appeal in health advertising — authentic pride ("I earned this through effort") and hubristic pride ("I'm superior") — against ads that primed either an independent or interdependent sense of self. Study 1 used sunscreen and skin health; Study 2 used flu vaccination. Authentic pride appeals worked better when the ad evoked an interdependent self-construal (seeing yourself in relation to others), while hubristic pride appeals worked better when the ad evoked an independent self-construal, with the authors identifying a serial chain of mediators explaining each match.
studies.why_it_matters: Pride is one of the most commonly used emotions in health and personal-care advertising, and this suggests the same prideful message can help or hurt depending on whether the surrounding creative frames the viewer as an individual or as part of a group.
studies.story_angle_primary: A prompt to audit pride-based creative for internal consistency: if the copy says "be the best," the imagery and framing probably need to be individualistic too, while "look after yourself for the people who need you" pairs with earned, effort-based pride. Worth A/B testing in live health campaigns before treating the match effect as settled.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shows how advertisers quietly tune which version of "you" they are speaking to — the self-made achiever or the family member — and why boastful messaging lands with some people and grates on others.
studies.caveats: Two controlled experiments with sample sizes and participant sources not reported in the abstract; self-construal was manipulated within the ad rather than measured in real audiences; outcomes are likely ad evaluations and intentions, not observed purchase or vaccination behavior; health categories only.
studies.verdict_notes: Both match effects are stated in the correct direction, the two study contexts (sunscreen/skin health; flu vaccination) are right, and the serial mediators are mentioned; missing Ns and outcome type are flagged in Caveats.

studies.title: Clever metaphors didn't beat plain language in a lottery's charity advertising
studies.paper_title: Literal and abstract metaphorical framing in public welfare lottery advertising: cognitive and affective responses in welfare communication
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a within-subjects experiment with 142 participants who each viewed two official Taiwan Public Welfare Lottery advertisements — one using literal, explicit messaging about where the money goes, the other using abstract metaphorical framing of social value. Across the main measures — understanding of the brand's welfare role, brand attitude and behavioral intention — there were no significant differences between the two framings. Modeling confirmed the expected cognition-to-attitude-to-intention chain, but the creative framing itself moved nothing at the construct level.
studies.why_it_matters: It is a rare published null result on a creative choice that agencies routinely treat as an upgrade: dressing a social-good message in metaphor did not outperform simply stating it.
studies.story_angle_primary: A caution against assuming that artful, metaphorical social-purpose creative earns its premium; the testable question is whether metaphor adds anything over plain explanation of where consumers' money goes, and this study says maybe not.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone who has watched a glossy, poetic charity or lottery ad and wondered what it was actually saying — the evidence here suggests the straightforward version communicates the social benefit just as well.
studies.caveats: Single country (Taiwan), single brand and category; 142 participants; within-subjects exposure means participants saw both ads, which can invite comparison effects; intentions rather than actual ticket purchases; item-level differences are explicitly flagged by the authors as exploratory.
studies.verdict_notes: Within-subjects design, N=142, the two official Taiwan lottery ads, the construct-level null result, the supported cognition–affect–behavior model and the authors' exploratory caution on item-level differences are all reported correctly.

studies.title: AR and VR ads moved the needle in Nepal — but only barely
studies.paper_title: The impact of virtual reality and augmented reality on global brand transformation: insights from immersive advertising among Nepalese adolescents
studies.journal: Young Consumers Insight and Ideas for Responsible Marketers
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 408 consumers aged 18 and over across five Nepalese cities after exposing them to real-world AR and VR brand content, then modeled the chain from perceived immersion to engagement and perceived diagnosticity (how well the content helped them judge the product), through brand attitude to purchase intention. All the expected links held, with brand attitude the strongest direct driver of purchase intention. The authors are unusually candid that the effects, while statistically significant, are small and come from passive exposure.
studies.why_it_matters: Immersive advertising is often pitched as a breakthrough format for emerging markets with first-time users; this gives a sober benchmark suggesting the gains are real but modest unless the content is genuinely interactive and informative.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat immersive formats as a brand-attitude play rather than a conversion lever, and note the authors' own point that passive exposure yields small effects — the open test is whether hands-on, product-demonstrating interactivity does materially better.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful corrective to the hype: putting on a headset or pointing a phone at a product changes how people feel about a brand only a little, and mostly by helping them understand the product better.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey — cannot establish causation; single country (Nepal); passive exposure design acknowledged by the authors; stated purchase intention rather than observed behavior; effect sizes small.
studies.verdict_notes: N=408, five Nepalese cities, 18+, the mediation chain, brand attitude as strongest direct predictor and the authors' candour about small effects and passive exposure are all accurate; two small framing stretches.

studies.title: ASMR ads may work least well on the people most sensitive to ASMR
studies.paper_title: When do consumers respond to ASMR-based retail advertising in Taiwan? The boundary role of ASMR responsiveness
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.the_study: A survey of 626 Taiwanese consumers on ASMR-based retail advertising, analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling, found that affective response and brand awareness predicted purchase intention — but that consumers' own ASMR responsiveness negatively moderated the affect-to-intention link, weakening rather than reversing it. A supplementary within-subject EEG pilot with 18 participants found no significant effects of ASMR exposure or cognitive load on frontal alpha activity, and the authors explicitly decline to treat it as confirmatory.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the assumption that tingle-inducing sensory advertising is universally persuasive, suggesting the sensory pleasure and the purchase decision can come apart — possibly most for the audience advertisers think of as the target.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are commissioning ASMR creative, the question to test is not whether listeners enjoy it but whether the sensory experience converts into brand evaluation — and whether your most ASMR-responsive viewers are the ones least likely to buy.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Explains why a whisper-and-crinkle ad can be deeply satisfying to watch and still leave you with no desire to buy the product: the pleasure may be the point, not the persuasion.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey — cannot establish causation; single country (Taiwan); self-reported purchase intention and "anticipated purchase behavior" rather than real purchases; the EEG component had only 18 participants and produced null results the authors themselves treat as descriptive; the hypothesized cognitive-load moderation was not supported.
studies.verdict_notes: N=626, PLS-SEM, the attenuating (not reversing) moderation, the unsupported cognitive-load moderation and the null 18-participant EEG pilot are all reported accurately; one story angle stretches the moderation into a purchase claim.

studies.title: "If only I had..." — when regret in an ad backfires
studies.paper_title: Communicating risk with narrative advertising: When protagonist regret helps or hurts persuasion
studies.the_study: Two experiments tested a common device in fear-appeal advertising: having the narrative's protagonist express regret after something bad happens ("If only I had bought insurance..."). Using insurance ad messages, researchers varied whether the protagonist voiced regret and measured how likely recipients thought the negative event was. Regret boosted persuasion only when people saw the event as unlikely; when they already perceived the risk as high, regret reduced effectiveness in Study 1 and trended the same way in Study 2. Narrative self-referencing — whether people mapped the story onto themselves — explained the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: Regret framing is standard in insurance, health and public-safety campaigns, but this suggests it only works on audiences who think "it won't happen to me" — and can weaken the message for audiences who already feel at risk.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audience risk perception may be the hidden variable in fear-appeal creative. Worth A/B testing regret-based narratives against neutral consequence narratives by segment — low-perceived-risk prospects versus high-risk ones — rather than assuming a single emotional formula travels across the whole target.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Those tearful "I wish I'd known" ads are engineered to make you picture yourself in the story. If you already worry about the risk, the regret pitch may land as hectoring rather than helpful — and research suggests it genuinely persuades you less.
studies.caveats: Two experiments in a single category (insurance advertising); sample sizes and recruitment not specified in the abstract; responses to ad messages rather than observed purchase of policies.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, direction and moderator all match the abstract, including the weaker Study 2 pattern and the narrative self-referencing mediator.

studies.title: Retargeted ads work better when you don't explain how they work
studies.paper_title: Online Ads That Follow Us from Site to Site—Are They Persuasive or Merely Annoying?
studies.journal: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a 4 × 2 between-subjects experiment crossing retargeting persistence (none, low, medium, high) with transparency (disclosing the targeting mechanism or not). Consumers who viewed the ad system as a "helper" delivering personally relevant information showed higher ad effectiveness and less ad avoidance. But adding transparency about how the targeting worked triggered surveillance concerns, undercutting that helper perception.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a measurable tension at the center of ad-tech policy: the disclosures meant to build trust can make the same ad feel like being watched rather than being helped.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test how "why am I seeing this ad?" disclosures are worded and where they sit. The finding suggests mechanism-level transparency can raise surveillance anxiety even when the targeting is accurate and useful — so brands may need wording that signals benefit and control rather than data plumbing, and should measure avoidance as well as click-through.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Those shoes that follow you across the internet aren't universally hated — in this experiment people often read persistent ads as useful. What flipped the feeling was being told how the tracking worked.
studies.caveats: Single online experiment with simulated ads; sample size and recruitment source not stated in the abstract; attitudinal and intended-avoidance measures rather than observed clicks or purchases; one product/ad context.
studies.verdict_notes: Headline and body assert that transparency undercuts helper perception/effectiveness; the abstract only reports that transparency triggers surveillance concerns. Caveat details (online, simulated ads) not in abstract.

studies.title: ESG only shows up in sales if you advertise it
studies.paper_title: Environmental, social, governance and sales in South Korean distribution industry
studies.journal: International Journal of Retail & Distribution Management
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed a decade of panel data (2012–2021) from 50 publicly listed South Korean wholesale and retail firms, pairing independent ESG ratings from the Korea Institute of Corporate Governance and Sustainability with firm sales, using fixed-effects regression. ESG performance on its own had no statistically significant effect on sales. The relationship only turned positive at higher advertising intensity, and among ESG's three pillars, only the social dimension interacted significantly with advertising. Effects were stronger for consumer-facing retailers than for wholesalers.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests ESG investment is not self-marketing: without communication spend behind it — and in categories where shoppers actually see the brand — sustainability performance left no trace in the top line.
studies.story_angle_primary: If the business case for ESG is being argued internally on sales grounds, this is evidence that the communications budget is part of the mechanism, not an optional add-on. Worth examining which ESG pillar your category's customers can even perceive — the social dimension carried the effect here, while environmental and governance did not.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Companies' sustainability records largely don't move shoppers unless the company spends to tell them about it — a reminder of how much of what consumers "know" about corporate virtue arrives via advertising.
studies.caveats: Single country and industry (South Korean wholesale/retail), only 50 firms; observational panel data, so the advertising–ESG–sales interaction is correlational, not causal; short-term sales outcomes only.
studies.verdict_notes: Panel size, years, ratings source, null direct effect, advertising-intensity moderation, social-dimension-only interaction and retail-vs-wholesale contrast all match; correlational caveat is present.

studies.title: Big influencers should talk big ideas; small influencers should sweat the details
studies.paper_title: Matching Mega and Nano Influencers with Ad Messages: How Construal Fit Drives Processing Fluency and Brand Outcomes
studies.journal: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
studies.the_study: Two online experiments with Prolific participants (N=436 and N=209) crossed endorser type (mega-influencer vs. nano-influencer) with ad message type (abstract, big-picture framing vs. concrete, specific framing). Brand attitudes and purchase intentions were highest when the pairing "fit": mega-influencers with abstract messages, nano-influencers with concrete ones. Processing fluency — how easily the ad felt to take in — mediated the effect, and mismatched pairings measurably dampened ad effectiveness.
studies.why_it_matters: Brands increasingly debate reach versus intimacy in influencer selection, but this suggests the creative brief matters as much as the follower count: the same copy can help or hurt depending on who delivers it.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit live influencer campaigns for construal mismatch — are nano-creators being handed brand-level aspirational scripts, and mega-creators asked to demo product specifics? Worth A/B testing message framing by creator tier rather than running one master script across the roster.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Explains the nagging sense that some sponsored posts feel "off": a small local creator waxing lyrical about changing the world lands badly, while the same person describing exactly how a product performed feels credible.
studies.caveats: Online panel (Prolific) participants responding to constructed ads rather than real purchases; stated brand attitudes and purchase intentions, not observed behavior; Study 2 N=209 is small once split across four conditions.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, Prolific samples (N=436, N=209), construal-fit interaction, processing-fluency mediation and mismatch penalty all match the abstract.

studies.title: Why the smartest geofenced ad may not be drawn around your own store
studies.paper_title: Catch Me if You Can! The Economic Analysis of Geofencing
studies.the_study: A game-theoretic modeling paper in *Information Systems Research* analyzes when location-based "geofenced" advertising beats conventional advertising, using a Hotelling market in which consumers differ both in location and in whether they already know the advertiser exists. The model finds geofencing wins on three fronts — market expansion, higher margins and lower ad spend — and identifies a positive link between fence radius and optimal price that prior work missed. Its headline proposal is "flexible geofencing": targeting zones drawn around other points of interest rather than the advertiser's own storefront, which the analysis shows raises profits, consumer surplus and overall welfare.
studies.why_it_matters: Most practitioners default to drawing a proximity radius around their own location; the analysis argues that the fence's placement, size and the price being advertised should be set jointly, and that awareness distribution across a city determines whether geofencing pays at all.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test geofences anchored to competitor locations, transit hubs or complementary venues against the standard store-centered radius, and examine whether discount depth is being set independently of fence size when the model says they should move together.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A glimpse of why that coupon pings your phone where it does — and why advertisers may increasingly be buying attention near places that have nothing to do with their own address.
studies.caveats: Analytical model only — no empirical data, field test or consumer sample; conclusions depend on the stylized Hotelling assumptions about consumer locations and awareness.
studies.verdict_notes: Faithful to the model's structure and conclusions; the three-advantage comparison is reported without the location-independent-awareness condition under which it was derived.

studies.title: Young luxury shoppers see through celebrity sustainability ads — unless the brand has already done the work
studies.paper_title: Co-creating sustainable luxury: how young consumers decode celebrity-endorsed sustainability through deep metaphor
studies.journal: Qualitative Market Research An International Journal
studies.the_study: Researchers used the Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique — image-based, metaphor-driven depth interviews — with 20 Millennial and Gen Z consumers reacting to a researcher-constructed celebrity-endorsed sustainable luxury advertisement. Participants welcomed ethical progress but expressed persistent ambivalence, demanding that symbolic storytelling be matched by visible corporate action. Celebrity endorsers were read as powerful but conditional credibility brokers, persuasive only when seen as authentic extensions of brand values; participants redefined luxury itself around ethical balance and collective responsibility rather than material exclusivity.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests sustainability storytelling in luxury can backfire as performance unless substantive practice precedes the campaign, and that endorser fit is judged on values alignment rather than fame.
studies.story_angle_primary: Sequence matters: consider whether verifiable ethical practice is in place before commissioning the campaign, and whether creative can acknowledge rather than paper over consumer ambivalence about buying luxury goods at all.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shows how skeptically younger consumers now decode a famous face attached to an eco-message — and how they are quietly rewriting what "luxury" is supposed to mean.
studies.caveats: Interpretive qualitative study, N=20, with findings transferable rather than generalizable; a single researcher-constructed ad, one endorser and one category; no behavioral or purchase data.
studies.verdict_notes: Method, N=20, single constructed ad and the ambivalence/conditional-credibility findings match; headline labels participants as "luxury shoppers," which the abstract does not establish.

studies.title: Scaring young people about disease doesn't work; making health feel like a lifestyle does
studies.paper_title: Integrating public health advertising and the health belief model to predict diabetes prevention intention: evidence from Indonesian young generations
studies.journal: International Journal of Pharmaceutical and Healthcare Marketing
studies.the_study: A cross-sectional survey of 500 Indonesian Millennials and Gen Z respondents tested how exposure to social media health advertising and government public health advertising relates to diabetes prevention intention, analyzed with PLS structural equation modeling. Both ad types predicted higher health literacy, with social media exposure the stronger of the two, and health literacy in turn fed perceived susceptibility, perceived severity and health consciousness. Health consciousness was the strongest predictor of prevention intention; perceived severity — how bad respondents thought diabetes was — had no significant direct effect.
studies.why_it_matters: Public health and pharma campaigns aimed at younger audiences often lead with the severity of the disease, but this points toward identity- and lifestyle-framed messaging delivered through social channels instead.
studies.story_angle_primary: For social marketing briefs, consider shifting budget and creative weight from severity-based warnings toward literacy-building, lifestyle-oriented content on social platforms — and measure whether the mechanism (health consciousness) actually moves.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A reminder that grim statistics about chronic illness rarely change what anyone eats; feeling like "a person who cares about health" does more work than being told how serious the disease is.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey — cannot establish causation; self-reported intentions rather than observed behavior; single country (Indonesia) and single condition (diabetes); online questionnaire sample of young respondents only.
studies.verdict_notes: All reported paths match the abstract; the headline states a causal conclusion from a cross-sectional survey of intentions, though the body and caveats are appropriately hedged.

studies.title: The background behind your product shot may be quietly costing you clicks
studies.paper_title: When contextual backgrounds backfire: a multi-study investigation of visual design effectiveness in digital marketing
studies.journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
studies.the_study: Researchers combined three studies: an audit of 1,000 Instagram posts from leading fast-moving consumer goods brands, a Facebook field experiment spanning 101,200 ad impressions, and a controlled experiment with 431 participants. The Instagram audit found brands split almost evenly—53% used contextual "product in use" backgrounds, 47% used plain neutral ones—suggesting no industry consensus. In the live Facebook test, contextual backgrounds lifted click-through rates for hedonic products by 0.06 percentage points (a 67% relative gain) but cut CTR for utilitarian products by 0.05 points (a 56% relative drop). The controlled experiment showed these effects only appeared among consumers with relevant product experience.
studies.why_it_matters: Creative decisions that look like pure aesthetics are measurably moving ad performance in opposite directions depending on what is being sold and who is seeing it. With AI tools now generating and optimizing ad backgrounds at scale, the rule "lifestyle imagery always wins" could be systematically destroying performance on half a brand's catalog.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit your own creative library the way these researchers audited Instagram: are you defaulting to lifestyle backgrounds across all SKUs? The field-experiment evidence suggests splitting creative by product type—context and usage scenes for pleasure-driven items, clean neutral shots for practical, function-driven ones—and feeding product-type and audience-experience signals into AI creative optimization rather than letting it optimize on engagement alone. Effect sizes here are fractions of a percentage point on one platform in one category, so treat it as a hypothesis to test in your own account, not a settled rule.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The styled kitchen scene behind a snack ad and the stark white background behind a cleaning product are not arbitrary—they are nudges tuned to how your brain processes that kind of purchase. And the study suggests the nudges only work on you if you already know the category: novices barely register the difference, while experienced buyers are the ones whose clicks shift.
studies.caveats: The field experiment ran on a single platform (Facebook) with fast-moving consumer goods; absolute CTR differences are tiny (hundredths of a percentage point) even if relative gains sound large. Click-through is a proxy for attention, not purchase. The moderation test relied on a controlled online experiment with 431 participants rather than real buying behavior, and the Instagram audit is descriptive only.
studies.verdict_notes: All three study designs, the 53/47 split, the 0.06pp/67% and 0.05pp/56% CTR effects and the experience moderation match the abstract; limitations are well flagged.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **Fit, not quality, keeps deciding whether creative works.** The previous run established congruence and processing fluency as the recurring mechanism (AI appeal–product–character fit, W7221595688; body-positive casting matching values rather than body type, W7222466110). This batch is dominated by it: "Clever ads make mass brands look cool — and do nothing for luxury ones" (W7225085686), "Bragging vs. earning it" (W7225225862), "Big influencers should talk big ideas; small influencers should sweat the details" (W7215042802, which names processing fluency as the mediator), "Crowded food ads make the food look more fattening" (W7212718074) and "The background behind your product shot may be quietly costing you clicks" (W7213441852).
- **Measurement proxies keep failing, now at the level of causal identification.** The prior digest's cluster — clutter versus recall (W7222550305), watch time versus sales (W7222936501), impressions versus sponsor recall (W7223185198), reach versus applicants (W7223181558) — is extended by "Your ad platform's own algorithm is corrupting its effectiveness numbers" (W4386473346), which argues the problem is not a mismatched metric but a broken overlap condition in observational lift estimation.
- **Purpose messaging still depends on something outside the ad.** "A short sustainability class changed how students responded to green advertising" (W7220917637) and "180,000 hotel reviews show Americans punish weak sustainability claims hardest" (W7223212068) are joined by "ESG only shows up in sales if you advertise it" (W7223183773) and "Young luxury shoppers see through celebrity sustainability ads — unless the brand has already done the work" (W7213545149): substantive practice and communications spend both have to be in place before the claim lands.
- **Privacy concern is triggered by how targeting is described, not whether it is accurate.** "Knowing you're being tracked makes some people block ads — and others lean in" (W7222483887) now has two mechanism-level companions: "When a chatbot says 'I,' personalized ads start to feel creepy" (W7224590363) and "Retargeted ads work better when you don't explain how they work" (W7225262891).

**Advances**

- **Disclosure research moves off AI and onto ad tech.** The last batch concentrated on AI-authorship labels (W7222851502, W7223070691, W7223243344). W7225262891 and W7224590363 transfer the same logic — the wording of a disclosure is the variable — to targeting-mechanism notices and conversational-AI copy, where disclosure is closer to being legally mandated.
- **Media-planning econometrics gets a share figure.** "A telecom's 174,000 ad records reveal threshold effects" (W7223172682) established nonlinear frequency returns within one firm and month; "Go dark for one quarter, lose a tenth of your market share" (W7139097509) scales the same question to 7,029 brand-quarters across 22 categories and attaches a number to continuity.

**Counterpoints**

- **Consumers may not police performative advertising at all.** The previous run's W7223212068 and W7223056505 both implied audiences detect and punish hollow inclusivity or green claims. "Rainbow washing worked — even on LGBTQIAPN+ consumers" (W7224213924) finds the targeted community struggled to identify the practice as inauthentic, and that negative press — not consumer vigilance — restored scrutiny. W7213545149 sits in between, with younger luxury consumers skeptical but conditionally persuadable.
- **Explaining the business model helps; explaining the plumbing hurts.** "'We're passing advertising revenue back to you' beats 'special offer'" (W7222624740) found that spelling out how ad money flows raised perceived legitimacy. W7225262891 finds that spelling out how the targeting works raises surveillance concern and undercuts the "helper" read. The reconciliation — transparency about money is reassuring, transparency about data is not — is worth stating explicitly.
- **Metaphor loses a round.** Congruence and metaphor have been treated as creative upgrades across both runs. "Clever metaphors didn't beat plain language in a lottery's charity advertising" (W7225346645) is a published null on exactly that premise, alongside "ASMR ads may work least well on the people most sensitive to ASMR" (W7223005849) and the candid small effects in "AR and VR ads moved the needle in Nepal — but only barely" (W7225266445).

**New themes**

- **Threat-based appeals underperform in both directions** — "'If only I had...' — when regret in an ad backfires" (W7213970602) and "Scaring young people about disease doesn't work; making health feel like a lifestyle does" (W7212126619). No prior-run analogue.
- **Where to draw the fence** — "Why the smartest geofenced ad may not be drawn around your own store" (W7214312085) is the first location-targeting economics paper across these runs.
- **AI-authored creative has largely vanished from this batch.** The previous digest was built around it (eight studies); here only W7224590363 touches conversational AI. Either the publication wave has crested or it has moved to journals outside this window — worth watching next run.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Six studies in this batch independently find that creative techniques the industry treats as upgrades only pay off when matched to the brand, the product or the viewer — and otherwise do nothing or actively hurt. Wit made mass brands look cool and did nothing for luxury ones (W7225085686); dense food layouts read as higher-calorie, helping indulgence products and hurting health ones (W7212718074); contextual backgrounds lifted click-through for hedonic products and cut it for utilitarian ones, and only among experienced buyers (W7213441852); pride appeals reversed depending on whether the ad framed the viewer as an individual or a group member (W7225225862); abstract messaging worked for mega-influencers and concrete for nano-creators, with mismatches measurably dampening effectiveness (W7215042802); and a lottery's metaphorical social-good creative beat plain explanation on nothing at all (W7225346645).

**Why pitch this now:** Generative tools are now producing and auto-optimizing ad variants at scale against engagement signals, with no knowledge of where a brand sits on the luxury ladder or whether a product is bought for pleasure or function — exactly the variables this evidence says flip the sign of the effect.

**Angle:** A reported feature arguing that there is no such thing as good creative in the abstract, only matched creative — and that the rules of thumb now being hard-coded into automated creative optimization ("lifestyle imagery wins," "humor builds affinity," "metaphor beats plain copy") are each demonstrably wrong for half a catalog. For creative directors, brand strategists and the people buying AI creative tooling, with a consumer-facing thread on how layouts and backgrounds act as unstated product claims.

**Potential headlines:**
- The same ad that lifts a mass-market brand quietly damages a luxury one
- Clever creative isn't better creative, and the evidence is piling up
- Your creative optimizer doesn't know what your brand is supposed to feel like

**Potential outlets:**
- **The Drum** — runs the creative-effectiveness argument at length and has an audience of creative leads who would contest the luxury-humor and metaphor-null findings on the record.
- **Adweek** — well placed for the collision between automated creative generation and brand-positioning judgment, with named agency and brand voices.
- **Harvard Business Review** — the framing that creative decisions are positioning decisions, not esthetic ones, suits its managerial register and its interest in where automation should not be given discretion.
- **Fast Company** — covers AI creative tooling and design decisions for a general business-design readership, and the visual-density and background findings are concrete enough to illustrate.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Go dark for one quarter, lose a tenth of your market share (Work ID W7139097509):** A single number — roughly 10% share lost for one dark quarter across 1,000-plus brands — that marketers can take into budget negotiations, for a marketing-trade news brief or a CMO-audience effectiveness column (flag the observational design and reverse-causality risk).
- **Clever ads make mass brands look cool — and do nothing for luxury ones (Work ID W7225085686):** Humor buys "coolness" only below the luxury line, making wit a challenger-brand tool rather than a universal one, for a creative-strategy trade feature or a consumer-psychology explainer on why prestige brands rarely joke.
- **Crowded food ads make the food look more fattening (Work ID W7212718074):** Visual busyness functions as an implicit calorie claim that either reinforces or contradicts positioning, for a food-and-beverage marketing explainer, with a strong consumer angle for a food or health section on delivery-app imagery.
- **When a chatbot says "I," personalized ads start to feel creepy (Work ID W7224590363):** Swapping "I" for "you" in highly personalized assistant copy is a near-free fix for privacy backlash — and buddy personas make it worse, for a conversational-commerce or adtech trade brief.
- **Rainbow washing worked — even on LGBTQIAPN+ consumers (Work ID W7224213924):** The targeted community could not reliably spot the inauthenticity, and press coverage rather than consumer vigilance was what broke the effect, for a brand-purpose trade feature or a general-interest piece on who actually polices Pride marketing (flag n=20/n=74, Brazil only).
- **Your ad platform's own algorithm is corrupting its effectiveness numbers (Work ID W4386473346):** The better a platform targets, the less its own observational lift numbers can be trusted — a direct argument for keeping randomized holdouts, for a media-measurement or adtech trade explainer.
- **Bragging vs. earning it (Work ID W7225225862):** Pride appeals only land when the surrounding creative frames the viewer the matching way, which makes internal consistency the testable variable in health campaigns, for a healthcare-marketing trade piece or a creative-strategy column.
- **Clever metaphors didn't beat plain language in a lottery's charity advertising (Work ID W7225346645):** A rare published null on a creative choice agencies charge a premium for, for a social-marketing or agency-accountability trade piece (flag single brand, 142 participants, within-subjects design).
- **AR and VR ads moved the needle in Nepal — but only barely (Work ID W7225266445):** A sober benchmark against immersive-format hype, with the authors themselves pointing to passive exposure as the limit, for an emerging-markets marketing brief or an immersive-tech trade explainer.
- **ASMR ads may work least well on the people most sensitive to ASMR (Work ID W7223005849):** Sensory pleasure and purchase intent come apart, possibly most in the audience brands are courting, for a consumer-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet (flag the 18-person EEG pilot's null results).
- **"If only I had..." — when regret in an ad backfires (Work ID W7213970602):** Regret-based fear appeals persuade people who think it won't happen to them and weaken the message for those who already feel at risk — a segmentation argument for insurance and public-safety campaigns, for an insurance-marketing or public-health communications piece.
- **Retargeted ads work better when you don't explain how they work (Work ID W7225262891):** Mechanism-level "why am I seeing this ad?" disclosures raise surveillance anxiety even when the targeting is genuinely useful, a live problem for regulators and platforms, for a privacy-and-adtech trade column or a policy-facing explainer.
- **ESG only shows up in sales if you advertise it (Work ID W7223183773):** Across a decade of Korean retail panel data, ESG performance moved sales only at high advertising intensity, and only via the social pillar — evidence that communications spend is part of the ESG business case, for a sustainability-business column or a retail-trade explainer.
- **Big influencers should talk big ideas; small influencers should sweat the details (Work ID W7215042802):** Running one master script across a creator roster creates measurable construal mismatch, for a creator-economy or influencer-marketing trade feature.
- **Why the smartest geofenced ad may not be drawn around your own store (Work ID W7214312085):** "Flexible geofencing" — fences anchored to competitor sites, transit hubs or complementary venues — plus a joint fence-size-and-price rule, for a retail-media or location-marketing trade explainer (flag that it is a model with no field data).
- **Young luxury shoppers see through celebrity sustainability ads — unless the brand has already done the work (Work ID W7213545149):** Millennial and Gen Z participants treated famous endorsers as conditional credibility brokers and redefined luxury around ethical balance, for a luxury-industry trade feature or a general-interest piece on how younger buyers are rewriting the meaning of luxury (flag N=20 qualitative).
- **Scaring young people about disease doesn't work; making health feel like a lifestyle does (Work ID W7212126619):** Perceived severity had no direct effect while health consciousness was the strongest predictor — a case for identity-framed social content over grim warnings, for a public-health communications piece or a pharma-marketing brief.
- **The background behind your product shot may be quietly costing you clicks (Work ID W7213441852):** A 101,200-impression field test showing lifestyle backgrounds lift hedonic products and depress utilitarian ones, with the effect confined to experienced category buyers, for an e-commerce or performance-marketing trade explainer (flag the hundredths-of-a-point absolute effects).

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Advertising — 2026-11-06
**Checked:** 2026-11-06 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: Go dark for one quarter, lose a tenth of your market share
**Work ID:** W7139097509 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Design detail not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "comparing market share for brands that advertised continuously against those that paused"
- **Abstract says:** "this large-scale study quantifies the cost of quarterly advertising stops, analysing 7,029 observations from over 1,000 brands across 22 product categories. On average, market share changed-10% after a single quarter of no advertising and-14% after four."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not describe the comparison design (continuous advertisers vs. pausers); it only reports average share change after pauses. The digest attributes a specific analytic structure that cannot be verified.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the study "quantified average market share change following quarterly advertising stops" and note the analytic approach is not described in the abstract (as the Caveats already hint)."

### Study 2: Clever ads make mass brands look cool — and do nothing for luxury ones
**Work ID:** W7225085686 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Crowded food ads make the food look more fattening
**Work ID:** W7212718074 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Fullness goals" rendered as "urge to splurge"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Dense layouts improved responses when more calories were desirable (indulgence goals, feeling the urge to splurge, indulgence-positioned products)"
- **Abstract says:** "higher visual density improves consumer responses when higher calories are desirable, such as under fullness or indulgence goals and for indulgence-positioned foods"
- **Problem:** The abstract names two distinct goal states — fullness (satiety) goals and indulgence goals. "Feeling the urge to splurge" restates indulgence rather than fullness, so one of the two named conditions disappears.
- **Suggested fix:** "Replace "feeling the urge to splurge" with "fullness/satiety goals" to match the abstract's two conditions."

### Study 4: When a chatbot says "I," personalized ads start to feel creepy
**Work ID:** W7224590363 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 5: Rainbow washing worked — even on LGBTQIAPN+ consumers
**Work ID:** W7224213924 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Country not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Two sequential Brazilian experiments compared a rainbow-washing ad against a neutral ad"
- **Abstract says:** "A hypothetical-deductive approach was used through two sequential experiments, comparing two advertisements (characterization of rainbow washing × neutral): first, exploratory (n = 20) ... and second, explanatory (n = 74)"
- **Problem:** The abstract never states the country of data collection. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop "Brazilian" or note that the country is inferred and not stated in the abstract."

**Issue B. "Reverse" overstates the media-coverage effect** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "prepare for the effect to reverse once coverage lands"
- **Abstract says:** "However, monitoring negative media repercussions related to the brand can enhance consumers’ critical thinking, thus mitigating this influence."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports mitigation (dampening) of the rainbow-washing effect, not a reversal into backlash. Advising brands to expect a reversal goes beyond the data.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "prepare for the effect to be dampened once negative coverage lands"."

**Issue C. Media exposure described as a manipulation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Exposure to negative media coverage about the brand restored some critical scrutiny and dampened the effect."
- **Abstract says:** "monitoring negative media repercussions related to the brand can enhance consumers’ critical thinking, thus mitigating this influence"
- **Problem:** The abstract's wording ("monitoring negative media repercussions") does not clearly indicate an experimental exposure manipulation; the digest presents it as one.
- **Suggested fix:** "Phrase as "awareness of negative media coverage about the brand was associated with more critical scrutiny, mitigating the effect"."

### Study 6: Your ad platform's own algorithm is corrupting its effectiveness numbers
**Work ID:** W4386473346 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 7: Bragging vs. earning it: which flavor of pride sells depends on how the ad makes you see yourself
**Work ID:** W7225225862 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 8: Clever metaphors didn't beat plain language in a lottery's charity advertising
**Work ID:** W7225346645 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 9: AR and VR ads moved the needle in Nepal — but only barely
**Work ID:** W7225266445 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Exposure described as researcher-administered** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Researchers surveyed 408 consumers aged 18 and over across five Nepalese cities after exposing them to real-world AR and VR brand content"
- **Abstract says:** "Data were collected from 408 consumers aged 18 years and above across five cities in Nepal who were exposed to real-world AR and VR brand marketing content."
- **Problem:** The abstract says participants had been exposed to real-world AR/VR content, not that the researchers administered the exposure; the digest implies a controlled exposure step in a design it elsewhere (correctly) calls cross-sectional.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as "surveyed 408 consumers ... who had been exposed to real-world AR and VR brand content"."

**Issue B. Interactivity condition not tested** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this gives a sober benchmark suggesting the gains are real but modest unless the content is genuinely interactive and informative"
- **Abstract says:** "Marketers should focus on designing interactive and easy-to-use content that clearly demonstrates product benefits."
- **Problem:** Interactivity is an authors' recommendation, not a tested moderator; the digest implies the study shows gains are larger with interactive content.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute it as the authors' recommendation rather than a finding ("the authors recommend interactive, benefit-demonstrating content")."

### Study 10: ASMR ads may work least well on the people most sensitive to ASMR
**Work ID:** W7223005849 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Moderation restated as lower purchase likelihood** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "whether your most ASMR-responsive viewers are the ones least likely to buy"
- **Abstract says:** "ASMR responsiveness negatively moderated the relationship between affective mechanism and purchase intention, indicating attenuation rather than reversal of the positive effect."
- **Problem:** The finding is that the affect-to-intention link is weaker among highly ASMR-responsive consumers, not that they have lower purchase intention or are less likely to buy.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as "whether, for your most ASMR-responsive viewers, enjoyment translates less strongly into purchase intention"."

### Study 11: "If only I had..." — when regret in an ad backfires
**Work ID:** W7213970602 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 12: Retargeted ads work better when you don't explain how they work
**Work ID:** W7225262891 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Transparency effect overstated** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "But adding transparency about how the targeting worked triggered surveillance concerns, undercutting that helper perception."
- **Abstract says:** "However, if the system is transparent about its targeting mechanism, it triggers surveillance concerns."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that transparency triggers surveillance concerns, but it does not state that transparency reduced the helper perception, lowered ad effectiveness or raised avoidance. The headline ("Retargeted ads work better when you don't explain how they work") and the consumer angle ("What flipped the feeling was being told how the tracking worked") assert an outcome the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say transparency about the targeting mechanism triggered surveillance concerns, and note that the abstract does not report whether this translated into lower effectiveness or higher avoidance; soften the headline accordingly."

**Issue B. Study context not stated in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Single online experiment with simulated ads; sample size and recruitment source not stated in the abstract"
- **Abstract says:** "we conducted a 4 (retargeting persistence: non-retargeting, low persistence, medium persistence, and high persistence) × 2 (transparency: absence and presence) between-subjects experiment"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not say the experiment was conducted online or that the ads were simulated, nor that there was a single product context (the digest also asserts "one product/ad context").
- **Suggested fix:** "Mark the online/simulated-ad and single-context details as unverifiable from the abstract."

### Study 13: ESG only shows up in sales if you advertise it
**Work ID:** W7223183773 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 14: Big influencers should talk big ideas; small influencers should sweat the details
**Work ID:** W7215042802 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 15: Why the smartest geofenced ad may not be drawn around your own store
**Work ID:** W7214312085 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Dropped modeling condition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The model finds geofencing wins on three fronts — market expansion, higher margins and lower ad spend"
- **Abstract says:** "We first compare geofencing and traditional advertising under location-independent awareness (i.e., informed consumers are uniformly distributed along the city). We show that geofencing outperforms the alternative for three reasons, namely, market expansion, profit-margin enhancement, and cost savings."
- **Problem:** The three-way advantage over traditional advertising is established in the location-independent-awareness case; the abstract separately notes that awareness distribution significantly affects when geofencing is applicable and profitable. The digest states the result unconditionally in the study summary.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add that the three advantages hold in the baseline case where informed consumers are uniformly distributed, and that profitability changes once awareness varies by location."

### Study 16: Young luxury shoppers see through celebrity sustainability ads — unless the brand has already done the work
**Work ID:** W7213545149 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Participants described as luxury shoppers** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Young luxury shoppers see through celebrity sustainability ads — unless the brand has already done the work"
- **Abstract says:** "an interpretive, ZMET-based study of 20 Millennial and Generation Z consumers responding to a single, researcher-constructed celebrity advertisement"
- **Problem:** The abstract describes Millennial and Gen Z consumers, not verified luxury buyers; the headline also implies a tested conditional effect ("unless the brand has already done the work") that is an interpretive implication rather than a measured contingency.
- **Suggested fix:** "Refer to "young consumers" and frame the brand-action condition as what participants demanded rather than a tested effect."

### Study 17: Scaring young people about disease doesn't work; making health feel like a lifestyle does
**Work ID:** W7212126619 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal headline on survey data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Scaring young people about disease doesn't work; making health feel like a lifestyle does"
- **Abstract says:** "A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 500 Indonesian Millennials and Generation Z respondents... Health consciousness emerged as the strongest predictor of diabetes prevention intention, followed by perceived susceptibility, while perceived severity showed no significant direct effect."
- **Problem:** The headline asserts what works and what does not, based on cross-sectional associations with stated prevention intention; perceived severity lacked a direct effect but was still enhanced by health literacy, and nothing in the study tested actual campaign exposure effects on behavior.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as an association, e.g. "Among young Indonesians, health consciousness predicted prevention intention — disease severity did not.""

### Study 18: The background behind your product shot may be quietly costing you clicks
**Work ID:** W7213441852 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Go dark for one quarter, lose a tenth of your market share | ⚠️ Minor issues | Headline numbers (-10%, -14%), sample (7,029 observations, 1,000+ brands, 22 categories) and the continuity/recency framing all match. One design detail is described more specifically than the abstract supports. |
| 2 | Clever ads make mass brands look cool — and do nothing for luxury ones | ✅ Accurate | Three experiments, the three categories, Brand X plus Honda/BMW, the coolness mechanism and the non-luxury-only boundary condition are all reported faithfully; intentions-vs-behavior and missing sample sizes are flagged in Caveats. |
| 3 | Crowded food ads make the food look more fattening | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study count (four experiments + one secondary data study), the density-to-perceived-calories effect and the two-sided moderation are correct; one moderator is mislabeled. |
| 4 | When a chatbot says "I," personalized ads start to feel creepy | ✅ Accurate | Both Ns, the personalization × grammatical-subject manipulation, the moderated mediation via privacy concern, the second-category replication and the friend-vs-servant boundary condition all match the abstract. |
| 5 | Rainbow washing worked — even on LGBTQIAPN+ consumers | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample sizes, sequential design, measures and the core finding are faithful; the country is not stated in the abstract and one story angle upgrades "mitigating" to "reversing". |
| 6 | Your ad platform's own algorithm is corrupting its effectiveness numbers | ✅ Accurate | The overlap-violation argument, the missing-data/matrix-completion framing, validation on simulated and real data and the targeting-efficiency claim all match; methodological nature is flagged in Caveats. |
| 7 | Bragging vs. earning it: which flavor of pride sells depends on how the ad makes you see yourself | ✅ Accurate | Both match effects are stated in the correct direction, the two study contexts (sunscreen/skin health; flu vaccination) are right, and the serial mediators are mentioned; missing Ns and outcome type are flagged in Caveats. |
| 8 | Clever metaphors didn't beat plain language in a lottery's charity advertising | ✅ Accurate | Within-subjects design, N=142, the two official Taiwan lottery ads, the construct-level null result, the supported cognition–affect–behavior model and the authors' exploratory caution on item-level differences are all reported correctly. |
| 9 | AR and VR ads moved the needle in Nepal — but only barely | ⚠️ Minor issues | N=408, five Nepalese cities, 18+, the mediation chain, brand attitude as strongest direct predictor and the authors' candour about small effects and passive exposure are all accurate; two small framing stretches. |
| 10 | ASMR ads may work least well on the people most sensitive to ASMR | ⚠️ Minor issues | N=626, PLS-SEM, the attenuating (not reversing) moderation, the unsupported cognitive-load moderation and the null 18-participant EEG pilot are all reported accurately; one story angle stretches the moderation into a purchase claim. |
| 11 | "If only I had..." — when regret in an ad backfires | ✅ Accurate | Design, direction and moderator all match the abstract, including the weaker Study 2 pattern and the narrative self-referencing mediator. |
| 12 | Retargeted ads work better when you don't explain how they work | ⚠️ Minor issues | Headline and body assert that transparency undercuts helper perception/effectiveness; the abstract only reports that transparency triggers surveillance concerns. Caveat details (online, simulated ads) not in abstract. |
| 13 | ESG only shows up in sales if you advertise it | ✅ Accurate | Panel size, years, ratings source, null direct effect, advertising-intensity moderation, social-dimension-only interaction and retail-vs-wholesale contrast all match; correlational caveat is present. |
| 14 | Big influencers should talk big ideas; small influencers should sweat the details | ✅ Accurate | Design, Prolific samples (N=436, N=209), construal-fit interaction, processing-fluency mediation and mismatch penalty all match the abstract. |
| 15 | Why the smartest geofenced ad may not be drawn around your own store | ⚠️ Minor issues | Faithful to the model's structure and conclusions; the three-advantage comparison is reported without the location-independent-awareness condition under which it was derived. |
| 16 | Young luxury shoppers see through celebrity sustainability ads — unless the brand has already done the work | ⚠️ Minor issues | Method, N=20, single constructed ad and the ambivalence/conditional-credibility findings match; headline labels participants as "luxury shoppers," which the abstract does not establish. |
| 17 | Scaring young people about disease doesn't work; making health feel like a lifestyle does | ⚠️ Minor issues | All reported paths match the abstract; the headline states a causal conclusion from a cross-sectional survey of intentions, though the body and caveats are appropriately hedged. |
| 18 | The background behind your product shot may be quietly costing you clicks | ✅ Accurate | All three study designs, the 53/47 split, the 0.06pp/67% and 0.05pp/56% CTR effects and the experience moderation match the abstract; limitations are well flagged. |

**Total issues:** 13 (11 Minor, 2 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 9
**Entries cleared:** 9
